prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "ANALOG DEVICES INC" (ticker ADI), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "ADI", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?

Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?

   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?

   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Analog Devices, Inc.
markets: Industrial (factory automation, instrumentation, aerospace and defense, healthcare, energy)
Automotive (battery management, in-cabin connectivity and audio, sensing)
Communications (wireless infrastructure, optical and data-center networking, AI data-center power)
Data converters, amplifiers, RF/microwave and power management ICs

mission.plain: ADI wants to connect the real, physical world (heat, sound, motion, electricity) to the digital world of computers, using its tagline "Ahead of What's Possible".

about.plain: Analog Devices makes tiny computer chips that let machines sense the real world, like temperature, sound, light, motion and electric power, and turn it into numbers a computer can use. It also makes chips that manage electric power and send signals by radio or cable. Its chips sit inside factory robots, cars, medical machines, cell towers and AI data centers. It sells about 75,000 different products to more than 100,000 customers.
about.customers: Mostly companies that build machines: factory-equipment makers, carmakers and their suppliers, telecom and data-center equipment makers, medical-device makers and defense contractors.
about.everyday: The chip that keeps an electric car's battery safe, or that helps a smartwatch read your heartbeat, may well come from Analog Devices.

money.plain: sensing, measuring and power chips for factories, test equipment, defense, healthcare and energy
battery-management, audio, connectivity and power chips for cars
chips for phones, wearables, hearing and audio gear
chips for cell towers, optical networks and data-center equipment
chips that feed power to AI processors, strengthened by buying Empower Semiconductor in July 2026
AI microcontrollers that let devices think locally, via the planned $1.35 billion Alif Semiconductor deal announced September 2026

result.summary: Yes. ADI has one of the strongest moats in semiconductors: its high-performance analog, converter and power chips are designed into customers' products for many years, are costly and risky to swap out, and rest on decades of hard-to-copy circuit-design and manufacturing know-how. Its huge catalogue of about 75,000 products sold to more than 100,000 customers spreads risk and supports gross margins above 60% (61.5% in FY2025, 67.3% in Q3 FY2026).

pricingPower.evidence: Industry press (EE Times China, via TrendForce) reported ADI raised prices on most products by about 15% on average from February 1, 2026 (up to 30% for military and high-reliability parts) and announced a second round from September 2026; ADI did not confirm the figures, but demand did not fall: Q3 FY2026 revenue rose 40% year on year to $4,021.9 million and GAAP gross margin rose to 67.3% from 61.5% for FY2025.

moats.evidence: ADI, together with Linear Technology (bought 2017) and Maxim Integrated (bought 2022), is the trusted name engineers pick for precision converters, amplifiers and power parts; it holds about 8,000 patents.

Once an ADI chip is designed into a car, factory system or medical device it usually stays for the product's whole life, often a decade or more, because replacing it means redesign and requalification (e.g., automotive and defense certification).
There is a mild ecosystem effect from its design tools, reference designs and EngineerZone community, but customers do not gain value from other customers using ADI chips.

With $11.0 billion of FY2025 revenue and a hybrid model of its own fabs plus foundry partners, ADI can spread $1.7 billion of yearly R&D across 75,000 products, though Texas Instruments has a larger, lower-cost 300mm analog manufacturing base.

Many high-performance niches (precision data converters, battery-management ICs, RF/microwave for defense) are small markets where only two or three suppliers can earn a return, so new entrants are rare.
ADI competes with the same business model as rivals like TI and Infineon; it does not benefit from a model incumbents cannot copy.
High-performance analog design depends on decades of accumulated designer experience and tight design-to-process tuning, which is why ADI with Linear and Maxim has led precision analog for 60 years.
ADI employs more than 13,000 engineers, including many of the industry's scarce senior analog designers, a skill that takes many years to develop.

customers.evidence: No public NPS data, but loyalty shows in long product lives and repeat design-ins: ADI serves more than 100,000 customers and its chips stay in customer products for many years, and orders rebounded strongly in 2026 (nine-month FY2026 revenue up 36%) despite reported price increases.

talent.evidence: ADI is a respected engineering employer with more than 13,000 engineers among about 24,000 staff in 31 countries, but it is not a fixture of top employer rankings and competes for chip talent with higher-paying AI-chip firms.

product.evidence: ADI is widely regarded as the leader in high-performance data converters, precision amplifiers and wireless battery-management systems, with the broadest portfolio after combining Linear Technology's power products and Maxim's automotive and power lines.

competitors.name: Texas Instruments Incorporated
competitors.note: Largest analog chip maker; competes across amplifiers, data converters, power management and embedded processors in industrial and automotive.

competitors.name: Infineon Technologies AG
competitors.note: Power semiconductors, automotive microcontrollers and AI data-center power delivery.

competitors.name: STMicroelectronics N.V.
competitors.note: Analog, power, sensors and microcontrollers for industrial and automotive.

competitors.name: NXP Semiconductors N.V.
competitors.note: Automotive battery-management, in-vehicle networking and industrial chips.

competitors.name: Microchip Technology Inc.
competitors.note: Analog and mixed-signal parts, microcontrollers and aerospace/defense chips.

competitors.name: Renesas Electronics Corporation
competitors.note: Analog and power (ex-Intersil, ex-Dialog) and automotive microcontrollers.

competitors.name: Monolithic Power Systems, Inc.
competitors.note: Power management ICs and modules, especially AI server and data-center power.

competitors.name: ON Semiconductor Corporation (onsemi)
competitors.note: Power semiconductors, image sensors and analog for automotive and industrial.

competitors.name: MACOM Technology Solutions Holdings, Inc.
competitors.note: RF, microwave and optical-network chips for defense, telecom and data centers.

competitors.name: Qorvo, Inc.
competitors.note: RF components for wireless infrastructure and defense.

competitors.name: Allegro MicroSystems, Inc.
competitors.note: Magnetic sensors and power ICs for automotive and industrial.

competitors.name: Vicor Corporation
competitors.note: High-density power modules for AI data centers, competing with ADI's power-delivery push.

competitors.name: SG Micro Corp
competitors.note: Chinese analog chip maker gaining share at the lower end of the Chinese market.

threats: Texas Instruments' large 300mm analog fabs give it a cost edge it can use to cut prices on catalogue parts.
Chinese analog makers (e.g., SG Micro) gaining share in China under localisation policies; China is a meaningful part of ADI's sales.
Cyclicality: FY2024 revenue fell 23% to $9.43 billion during an industrial and automotive inventory correction, and the 2026 boom could reverse.
Reported 2026 price rises could invite customers to qualify second sources if supply loosens.
Integration and execution risk from buying digital and power-delivery businesses (Empower in 2026, Alif pending) outside ADI's analog core.
Export controls and tariffs affecting sales to China and supply-chain costs.

ceo.name: Vincent Roche
ceo.background: Electronics engineer (B.S. in Electronic Systems; honorary Doctor of Science from the University of Limerick); joined ADI in 1988, President in 2012, CEO in 2013 and also Chair since 2022.

c1.evidence: ADI is a leader in high-performance analog, a large but mature industry; it is now riding fast-growing niches such as AI data-center communications (Q3 FY2026 communications revenue up 84% year on year).

c2.evidence: Engineers choose ADI for best-in-class precision and performance plus a 75,000-product catalogue and design support, and once designed in, its chips stay for many years, an advantage built over 60 years that is hard to copy.

c3.evidence: Ordinary consumers rarely know the name; ADI is well known only among engineers, where it is a default choice for precision converters but shares leadership of analog with Texas Instruments.

c4.evidence: ADI repeatedly stresses bridging the physical and digital worlds ("Ahead of What's Possible", now "Physical Intelligence") and backs it with $1.7 billion of yearly R&D, but it publishes no single word-for-word mission statement and its messaging is largely commercial.

c6.evidence: "precise, high-quality, engineering-driven"; among engineers and investors the impression is mostly positive, while the general public has little awareness of the company.

c7.evidence: ADI's markets grow with secular trends in automation and robotics, vehicle electrification, AI data centers and energy, helping lift nine-month FY2026 revenue 36% year on year to $10,805.6 million.

c8.evidence: ADI is expanding into AI-processor power delivery (Empower Semiconductor, completed July 2026) and edge AI processing (planned $1.35 billion Alif Semiconductor deal announced September 2026), widening its addressable market beyond analog.

m1.evidence: Roche has articulated a long-term vision of the "Intelligent Edge" and "Physical Intelligence" and built the portfolio toward it through acquisitions, though he is a strategist rather than a widely cited tech visionary.

m2.evidence: Not a founder, but a lifer who joined ADI in 1988 and has run it since 2013 with long-term, multi-decade bets like the Linear and Maxim mergers.

m4.evidence: There is no strong public evidence either way of a distinctive servant-leadership style by Roche.

m5.evidence: ADI keeps a strong engineering culture with more than 13,000 engineers and has preserved Linear's and Maxim's design teams, but the culture is not widely seen as uniquely inventive versus peers.

m6.evidence: Roche holds a degree in electronic systems and spent his career in ADI's technical and business-unit roles before becoming CEO.

m7.evidence: Roche frames ADI's work around benefits to society and the planet (health, energy, climate) and serves on industry and MIT advisory boards, with no known controversies, though there is little standout evidence beyond normal stewardship.

m7b.evidence: No record found of Roche giving a commencement speech at Stanford, Harvard, MIT or a similar top university; he holds an honorary doctorate from the University of Limerick.

m8b.evidence: Roche is a low-profile, understated executive rather than a celebrity CEO.

m9.evidence: Under Roche, ADI bought Hittite (2014), Linear Technology (2017) and Maxim (2022) and grew revenue from $2.7 billion in FY2012 to $11.0 billion in FY2025, with record revenue of $4,021.9 million in Q3 FY2026.

m10.evidence: ADI is not publicly known for notable frugality, though it runs a disciplined hybrid manufacturing model and returns most free cash flow to shareholders.

c10.evidence: ADI chips improve many lives indirectly, in medical equipment, car safety and battery systems, factory automation and communications networks, but as hidden components rather than products people use directly.

p2.evidence: High-performance analog and mixed-signal design is notoriously hard, depending on rare engineering skill, and ADI's chips are essential to measuring and powering everything from AI data centers to medical devices.

f1.evidence: Revenue rose in four of the last five years, from $5,603.1 million in FY2020 to $11,019.7 million in FY2025, with one drop in FY2024 ($9,427.2 million from $12,305.5 million) during an inventory correction.

f2.evidence: GAAP gross margin fell from 65.9% in FY2020 to 61.5% in FY2025 and operating margin was roughly flat (26.7% to 26.6%), weighed by Maxim acquisition amortization, though Q3 FY2026 margins rebounded to 67.3% and 40.1%.

f3.evidence: At August 1, 2026 ADI had $9,121.6 million of debt against $2,325.0 million of cash and short-term investments, but debt is under two years of trailing free cash flow ($4,937.5 million) and shareholders' equity was $33,815.8 million at FY2025 year-end.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from $1,498.2 million in FY2020 to $2,932.5 million in FY2025 and operating cash flow from $2,008.5 million to $4,812.2 million, despite a dip in FY2024.

v1.evidence: In precision data converters and battery-management chips ADI is often the performance leader (engineers pick it for accuracy), but in broad analog Texas Instruments is a close alternative, so it is not clearly best across the board.

v2.evidence: ADI is a well-regarded engineering employer but does not appear prominently in major employer rankings such as Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For.

c5.evidence: If ADI vanished, makers of cars, medical scanners, factory robots, cell towers, defense systems and AI data centers would face shortages of hard-to-replace chips, since many designs depend on ADI parts with no drop-in substitute.
